passages.t: Surrounded: ‘But You, O LORD, are a shield’
passages.happening:
The heading sets the scene: “A Psalm of David, when he fled from his son Absalom” (verse 1).

Then the prayer begins with a crowd of enemies. “O LORD, how my foes have increased! How many rise up against me!” (verse 1). Worse than their numbers is what they say: “Many say of me, ‘God will not deliver him’” (verse 2).

Then the psalm turns. “But You, O LORD, are a shield around me, my glory, and the One who lifts my head” (verse 3). The man cries out, and God hears: “To the LORD I cry aloud, and He answers me from His holy mountain” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
A heading is a short line above a psalm. This one names a moment told in 2 Samuel 15 to 18. David's son Absalom won the people's hearts, had himself made king, and marched on Jerusalem. David fled the city on foot, weeping. Whether David wrote the psalm on that day, or later readers linked it to that day, is a question the book page on the Psalms explains. Either way, the heading asks you to hear this prayer in the mouth of a king running from his own son.

The enemies' taunt is the cruellest part. They do not only say he will lose. They say God has given up on him. On the road out of Jerusalem a man called Shimei shouted almost exactly that (2 Samuel 16:8).

A shield was a soldier's first defence. A shield ‘around me’ means God covers him on every side.

‘The One who lifts my head’ is a Hebrew way of speaking. A person in shame walks with head bowed or covered. To lift someone's head is to give back his honour, as Pharaoh did when he restored his cupbearer (Genesis 40:13). David had left Jerusalem with his head covered (2 Samuel 15:30). God lifts it.

‘His holy mountain’ is Zion in Jerusalem, where the ark of God was kept. David had sent the ark back to the city as he fled (2 Samuel 15:25). He is cut off from the place, but not from the God who answers from it.

‘Selah’ follows verses 2 and 4. It is a word for the music or the singing whose exact meaning is not known. Many readers pause there.
passages.later:
The story behind the heading is told in 2 Samuel 15 to 18. It ends with Absalom's death and David's grief: “O my son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you” (2 Samuel 18:33).

The taunt that God will not save returns at the cross. Matthew records the leaders mocking Jesus: “He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him” (Matthew 27:43). Those words are closest to Psalm 22:8.

Paul asks the question this psalm answers: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31).
passages.asks:
The hardest voice in the psalm is the one that says, ‘God will not deliver him.’ Ask whether you hear that voice, about yourself or about someone else. The psalm does not argue with it. It turns and speaks to God: ‘But You, O LORD.’

You can make that same turn, in your own words or in the psalm's.

passages.happening:
Now comes something surprising. With enemies all around, the man sleeps. “I lie down and sleep; I wake again, for the LORD sustains me” (verse 5). “I will not fear the myriads set against me on every side” (verse 6).

Then he asks God to act. “Arise, O LORD! Save me, O my God! Strike all my enemies on the jaw; break the teeth of the wicked” (verse 7).

The psalm ends with a confession and a prayer for everyone: “Salvation belongs to the LORD; may Your blessing be on Your people” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Many call Psalm 3 a morning prayer, because of verse 5: he lay down, slept, and woke. For someone being hunted, to sleep at all is an act of trust. Waking up alive is a gift.

‘Myriads’ means tens of thousands, a huge number.

‘Arise, O LORD’ is an old cry. When Israel carried the ark through the wilderness, Moses would say, “Rise up, O LORD! May Your enemies be scattered” (Numbers 10:35). It means: come, act, as you did before.

‘Deliver’ in verse 2 and ‘salvation’ in verse 8 come from the same Hebrew word. The enemies said there was no salvation for him in God. The psalm ends, ‘Salvation belongs to the LORD.’ The last word answers the first taunt.

And the last line widens the prayer. A king who began with ‘me’ ends with ‘Your people’, praying a blessing on them, even though many of them had turned against him.
passages.later:
Jesus slept in a boat in a storm while his friends panicked (Mark 4:38). Peace in danger is a sign of trust in the Father.

Jonah, from inside the fish, ends his prayer with almost the same words as verse 8: “Salvation is from the LORD” (Jonah 2:9). And in Revelation a great crowd from every nation cries, “Salvation to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb” (Revelation 7:10).

Jesus told Peter to put away his sword (Matthew 26:52). And Peter later wrote that when Jesus suffered, “He made no threats, but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23).
passages.hard:
‘Strike all my enemies on the jaw; break the teeth of the wicked.’ Can someone who follows Jesus pray this?

First, see what the picture means. In the psalms the wicked are often pictured as wild animals with teeth (as in 58:6). To break a lion's teeth is to make it harmless. This is a prayer that God would stop the violent from doing harm. It asks God to act. It does not ask the man to take revenge himself.

Second, remember the story. The enemies here were led by David's own son. When Absalom was killed, David wept and wished he had died in his place (2 Samuel 18:33). A man can pray for rescue from a violent rebellion and still love the person who leads it.

Third, Christians read such prayers beside Jesus' command: “love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). Many hold that a cry for God to stop the violent is still right, while the follower of Jesus also prays for the good of those same enemies.

The harder curses in the Psalms, and the main ways Christians have read them, are set out in the part on the cursing psalms on the book page. None of those readings gives anyone permission to harm another person.
passages.asks:
Ask what keeps you awake. The psalm does not pretend the danger is small. It says ‘myriads’. And yet the man sleeps, because the LORD holds him up.

Tonight, before you sleep, name what you fear to God. Then hand it over. ‘Salvation belongs to the LORD’: it is his work, not yours.
